review: 3:1–2 רֻחַצְנוּ בַּדָּם — the Arabic غُسِلْنَا بِالدَّمِ is Rev 1:5 (הַמְרַחֵץ אֹתָנוּ מֵחֲטָאֵינוּ בְּדָמוֹ) with Rev 7:14; the Hebrew uses the passive of רָחַץ and keeps the blood as the means, so washing and blood stay in one breath as they do in the Greek.

3:3–4 וְלִמְלָכִים נַעֲשֵׂינוּ — Rev 1:6 (וַיַּעַשׂ אֹתָנוּ מְלָכִים); the Hebrew keeps the plural 'kings' rather than 'a kingdom', because the Arabic مُلُوكًا is plural and the stanza's point is the dignity of the washed.

4:2 כָּל־עוֹד אַתָּה שָׁם — the Arabic طَالَمَا أَنْتَ هُنَاك is 'as long as You are there'; the Hebrew keeps the temporal clause with כָּל־עוֹד, and the 'there' is left unspecified as the Arabic's هُنَاك is, so the line points at the table rather than at heaven.

4:3–4 נְקַוֶּה … וְנִרְאֶךָ — the Arabic نَتَرَجَّى أَنْ تَجِيءَ … فَنَرَاك is hope followed by sight; קָוָה is the psalm's waiting verb (Ps 130:5, קִוִּיתִי יְהוָה) and רָאָה is kept for the beatific sight (Job 19:27, וּמִבְּשָׂרִי אֶחֱזֶה), so the stanza ends in seeing, not merely in arriving.

1:1–2 נָשִׂיא … הַנִּשָּׂא — the Hebrew plays on the same root (נָשִׂיא / נִשָּׂא) because the Arabic pairs رَبَّنَا with السَّامِي; the pun is deliberate and is the reason the first line ends on 'prince' rather than 'Lord', which the next line's 'Your lofty name' then answers.
